analysis.one_liner: Bans the sale and possession of semiautomatic assault weapons and large-capacity ammunition magazines.
analysis.headline: The bipartisan assault-weapons ban cleared a Senate subcommittee and had hearings, but the full Judiciary Committee never voted, and it died when the 101st Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it a federal crime to sell, import, transfer, or possess semiautomatic assault weapons — naming models like the Kalashnikov, Uzi, AR-15, and TEC-9 — and magazines holding more than ten rounds. People who already owned one of the named guns would have had to register it within 30 days, and owners of large-capacity magazines would have had to sell or donate them to the government within 60 days. It also added a mandatory five-year prison term for anyone using an assault weapon during a violent or drug-trafficking crime.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone exposed to gun violence, since the stated purpose is "to control the sale and use of assault weapons" [S3]: the bill would have taken the most lethal semiautomatic rifles and pistols off the civilian market, banned magazines holding more than ten rounds, and let the Treasury Secretary act immediately with 90-day emergency import bans when a potentially dangerous firearm surfaced [S2] [S3]. Police and communities would no longer face those weapons in civilian hands [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Makes it a federal crime to transfer, import, transport, ship, receive, or possess any assault weapon and any detachable magazine or belt holding more than ten rounds, with exceptions only for government entities and lawful prior possession.

Names the specific weapons to be banned — Kalashnikov, Uzi, Mac 10/11, TEC-9 and TEC-22, Ruger Mini-14, AR-15, FN-FAL, Steyr Aug, Street Sweeper shotguns, and copies sold under other names — so manufacturers could not dodge the ban with a rebrand.

Requires the Treasury Secretary to identify additional assault weapons within 30 days of enactment, keep the list updated, and issue emergency orders of up to 90 days barring import and sale of firearms that may qualify — closing the door on copycat guns.
Adds a mandatory five-year prison term, stacked on top of any other sentence, for using or carrying an assault weapon during a violent or drug-trafficking crime.
Grandfathers people who lawfully owned the named guns, but only if they registered them within 30 days — putting the existing stock on a federal registry rather than leaving it untracked.

analysis.who_pays: Firearms manufacturers and importers lose the ability to sell the named product lines, and dealers lose that inventory. People who already owned one of the designated guns had to register it within 30 days or face the new possession ban, and owners of large-capacity magazines had to sell or donate them to a government entity within 60 days — property that was legal the day before would have become contraband [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun makers, dealers, and owners of listed weapons

drawbacks.text: The banned list reached popular civilian rifles: it designated the Ruger Mini-14 and AR-15, both widely sold semiautomatics, so many owners of ordinary rifles would have had to register with the federal government just to keep property they already owned.

It gave the Treasury Secretary sweeping authority to declare any additional semiautomatic firearm an assault weapon within 30 days of enactment and to impose emergency 90-day import and sales bans — broad power over an entire product category placed in one executive official's hands.

Owners of large-capacity magazines got only 60 days to sell or donate them to the government before possession became a federal crime — a surrender requirement on previously legal property that did not apply to the grandfathered guns.

The registration requirement turned otherwise lawful possession into a federal offense if the paperwork deadline was missed — the standard objection from gun owners' groups, who argued such laws burden people who follow the rules rather than those who do not.

The mandatory five-year sentence for using an assault weapon in a violent or drug-trafficking crime stacks on top of existing sentences, part of the era's escalating drug-war penalties rather than a narrowly targeted rule.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core of the bill — taking rapid-fire semiautomatic weapons and high-round-count magazines out of civilian commerce — is a real public-safety gain, and naming the weapons by model prevented easy workarounds. The honest cost side: coverage of the Ruger Mini-14 and AR-15 swept in rifles many Americans owned for ordinary purposes, and the Treasury Secretary's open-ended designation power, plus a 60-day magazine turn-in, went well beyond a narrow ban. A more carefully drawn list and a longer grandfathering period would have blunted the strongest objections without giving up the core restriction.

outcome.mechanism: The bill cleared its Senate Judiciary subcommittee and had hearings, but the full committee never voted, and it died when the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Senator Howard Metzenbaum introduced the Assault Weapon Control Act of 1989 on February 8, 1989, joined by Senators Chafee, Pell, and Cranston — including one Republican — giving the bill a bipartisan start.
It was read twice and referred to the Judiciary Committee, which sent it to its Subcommittee on the Constitution on February 24, 1989.
On April 19, 1989, the subcommittee approved the bill for full committee consideration with a substitute amendment — notably, without a recommendation.
The subcommittee held hearings on May 5, 1989, printed as S.Hrg. 101-507.
After those hearings, no further action was ever recorded: the full Judiciary Committee never voted on the bill, the Senate never voted, and it died when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Firearms manufacturers and importers kept selling the named rifles and pistols, and existing owners never had to register them or surrender large-capacity magazines.

for.name: Howard Metzenbaum
for.what_they_did: Sponsored and introduced the bill, and was the lead advocate moving it through the Judiciary subcommittee process.

for.name: John Chafee
for.what_they_did: One of the four original sponsors, giving the gun-restriction bill a Republican lead co-signer on day one.

for.name: Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on the Constitution
for.what_they_did: Approved the bill for full committee consideration with a substitute amendment in April 1989 and held hearings the following month.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee (chaired by Joseph Biden)
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to a committee vote after the subcommittee approved it in April 1989; no committee action appears in the record after the May 1989 hearings, and the bill died there.

against.name: National Rifle Association
against.what_they_did: Fiercely opposed assault-weapon restrictions in this period, rallying members against registration and bans and pressuring lawmakers of both parties to keep such bills off the floor.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan from the start — a Republican senator helped introduce it, and the 12 cosponsors included 10 of 55 Senate Democrats and 1 of 45 Senate Republicans — but no vote was ever recorded, so the chamber's actual split is unknown.

industries.note: The bill bans the sale and import of a specific product line — Kalashnikov, Uzi, AR-15, TEC-9 and other named semiautomatics — and lets the Treasury Secretary add more, eliminating revenue from the segment of the market these firms profit from most. The industry's interest in blocking the bill ran directly against the public-safety purpose.
Dealers would lose the ability to stock or sell the designated weapons and large-capacity magazines, and would bear record-keeping tied to the registration requirement for grandfathered guns.

industries.industry: Owners of affected firearms and magazines
industries.note: People who already lawfully owned the named guns could keep them only by registering within 30 days, and magazine owners had to sell or donate them to the government within 60 days — a real cost to a large group of constituents, which is why the bill was politically hard to move.
